# ub-mode

Follow three phases in small, verifiable units: first make it work, then make
it right, then follow practice. Use these principles to guide judgment within
the requested scope. User instructions and repository rules govern permissions,
validation, and delivery; this skill does not expand them. Preserve unrelated
work. A request to inspect, explain, or propose does not authorize implementation.

This is a personal adaptation of the author's document supplied by the user.
The unchanged [original](references/original.md) is retained for comparison and
future updates; it is source material, not an additional set of active rules.

## First make it work

- Keep one decision in one place. Make the smallest cohesive edit that solves
  the problem. Subtract unnecessary complexity before adding more.
- Get the data shape and invariants right before the logic. Do prerequisite
  work that simplifies later phases first.
- For a behavior change, write a meaningful failing test, observe the expected
  failure, and make the smallest change that passes. If an honest test is
  impractical, explain the limitation and use appropriate direct verification.
  Do not invent tests for documentation or trivial reversible edits.
- Consider what the design would look like if the requirement had existed
  from the start. Deliver the needed change in reversible pieces; avoid
  speculative rewrites beyond the user's request.
- When two fixes relying on the same premise fail the same check, pause that
  approach. State the premise, reproduce the failure, identify the actors and
  state owners involved, and correct the false assumption or misplaced ownership
  before attempting another variation. Do not mechanically remove an assignment
  without understanding its role.
- Aim at an observable end state. An intermediate break is acceptable when
  planned, bounded, reversible, and resolved before delivery.
- When repeated or complex work benefits from a tool, do one representative
  unit by hand, then make the tool reproduce the checked result. Keep one-off
  straightforward work simple.

### Architecture and boundaries

- Model domain concepts and invariants in the data and types so invalid states
  are difficult or impossible to construct. Reuse clear, local code; avoid
  extra abstractions that do not enforce a useful invariant.
- Keep terminology consistent. Maintain or extend a domain glossary when
  ambiguity warrants one; do not create documentation merely to satisfy a step.
- Validate and parse outside data once at its boundary. Inside that boundary,
  trust the validated representation. Keep business rules in pure functions
  where practical. Do not silence the compiler to conceal a type error.
- Avoid shared mutable state when actors do not need it. If sharing is required,
  give it one enforced writer or explicit synchronization and ownership.
- Make retryable operations idempotent, including recovery from partial failure.
  Where repetition has a distinct effect, define the retry and deduplication
  behavior explicitly.

## Then make it right

- Reproduce defects and fix their causes. A guard that hides a broken invariant
  is insufficient; legitimate boundary validation still belongs at the boundary.
- Finish and verify one small unit before starting the next. Follow the current
  repository's focused test and lint rules. Reuse valid results; do not launch
  whole-repository suites for a scoped correction unless the selected repository
  gate or user request requires them.
- Test observable behavior through the interface its consumer uses. Assertions
  should fail when the promised behavior is removed or broken.
- Before refactoring, pin the existing behavior. Change the structure, then
  verify that the behavior is preserved.

### Use the shared quality tools

The tools are installed outside examined repositories under
`/Users/dimitri/.local/share/unclebob/`. Read the relevant
[shared usage notes](/Users/dimitri/.local/share/unclebob/local/README.md) and each
tool's help rather than guessing flags. Keep reports and worker output locally
ignored. Do not add these personal tools to project manifests or CI.

Scope analysis to changed functions/files and directly affected behavior.
Use available language support and explain missing tooling or measurement;
do not substitute a different metric and label it as the requested one.

- **Crapper:** use CRAP below 10 as an improvement target for changed functions
  when valid coverage is available. A complexity-only report is not a CRAP
  score. Improve cohesion and meaningful coverage; do not split a function or
  case statement merely to move complexity out of the reported function.
  Record existing findings outside the authorized scope instead of silently
  expanding the task.
- **Dryer:** review similarity candidates scoring 0.8 or above. Consolidate code
  when it represents the same responsibility or rule. Similar structure alone
  does not justify coupling independent concepts through a shared abstraction.
- **Mutator:** run against changed behavior with an explicit focused test
  command. Investigate uncovered mutants and survivors, add meaningful coverage,
  and remove code demonstrated to be dead. Classify equivalent or invalid
  mutants and measurement limitations. Set a bounded scope and runtime; report
  unresolved results rather than weakening tests or claiming a perfect score.

Repository validation instructions remain the command authority. For the Layout
Editor, consult its [Validation Lanes](/Users/dimitri/Documents/Code/personal/glove80/layout-editor/app/docs/references/validation-lanes.md);
other repositories use their own guidance.

For a saved assessment using Dagu `collect-ub`, read the
[UB findings-source interface](references/findings-source.md). It consumes the
caller's branch scope, retains measurements and evaluated findings, and starts
no corrections.

## Follow practice

- Keep a concise record of meaningful actions, reasons, checks, results, and
  unresolved issues. Summarize it on completion; use chat or a requested local
  artifact rather than adding an unsolicited tracked log.
- Keep the main context focused. Read supporting material as needed and retain
  useful summaries. Delegate only when authorized and beneficial, with bounded
  ownership and integration responsibility.
- Clean up temporary worktrees created for this task only after checking that
  no process or ongoing task needs them and that their work is preserved.
  Leave uncommitted work intact pending a decision. Keep broader cleanup
  separate from an unrelated implementation request.
- Commit only when authorized, using small, ordered, reviewable commits that
  explain why, what changed, and how it was verified. A commit request does not
  authorize a push. Push, merge, or publish only within the user's explicit
  authorization and repository branch workflow; never infer a push to main.
  Honor local-only and no-commit instructions. Reuse authorization already given
  for the same action instead of asking again.
